---
title: Relational prediction
description: "Build a decision-time observation from an entity, related records, as-of lookups, and nested histories."
engine: markdown
---

A racing team wants to prioritize reliability reviews before an upcoming race.
Its database holds drivers, entries, race results, constructors, circuits, and
pit stops. Each earlier result can keep its circuit, constructor, and pit
stops attached, so the model can test whether those relationships help.

RelBench's [racing tasks](https://huggingface.co/datasets/stanford-star/relbench-v1/blob/main/rel-f1/README.md)
include future non-finishes, finishing positions, and top-three qualifying
outcomes. The example below adapts the entity-and-related-records pattern to
a hypothetical pre-race application with its own cohort and label definition.

## Define one entry and its cutoff

Prepare one observation per driver entry in a specified upcoming race, using
the entry list known at the decision time. For this example the cutoff is
June 5, 2026 at noon UTC, before a race scheduled for June 7. The team scores
the entries to choose where to spend its review capacity.

The Boolean `retired_next_race` describes whether that entry receives an
official retirement result in that race. Map the application's result codes
to this label explicitly: a classified finish, including a lapped finish, is
false; a did-not-start result is also false for this particular retirement
question. A cancelled race or missing final result leaves the label unavailable.
Assess non-starts separately if they also matter to the decision.

Retain the driver, race, and cutoff keys outside the model to associate every
output with its entry. A training label becomes usable only after the final
result is available. Upcoming circuit and constructor information may be inputs
when already known at the cutoff; the upcoming race's result and pit stops may
not.

## Join related tables into one observation

The application controls joins, availability, and multiplicity:

| Source relation | Role in one entry observation |
|---|---|
| Driver and upcoming entry | Root attributes known at the cutoff |
| Earlier results for the driver | One repeated record per earlier result |
| Race, circuit, and constructor referenced by a result | Attributes looked up into that result's record |
| Pit stops belonging to an earlier result | A repeated child collection under that result |
| Final upcoming-race result | A later label, excluded from the inputs |

Resolve each many-to-one lookup to one row with the values available at the
cutoff. Group pit stops beneath their result before collecting results; a
flat join would duplicate a result once for every stop. Keep each result's
fields aligned when ordering or limiting histories.

This illustrative record contains two earlier results. Every result and pit
stop was available at the June 5 cutoff; the root label was attached later:

```yaml
driver_nationality: British
upcoming_circuit: lakeside
constructor: team-7
past_results:
  - occurred_at: "2026-05-10T12:00:00Z"
    age_days: 26
    circuit: hill-park
    constructor: team-7
    grid_position: 8
    finishing_position: 6
    retired: false
    pit_stops:
      - lap: 19
        duration_seconds: 23.7
      - lap: 42
        duration_seconds: 24.1
  - occurred_at: "2026-05-24T12:00:00Z"
    age_days: 12
    circuit: coast-ring
    constructor: team-7
    grid_position: 7
    finishing_position: 18
    retired: true
    pit_stops:
      - lap: 15
        duration_seconds: 27.8
retired_next_race: false
```

## Describe the nested records

Declare field types and nested collections to match that prepared observation.
Each branch can contain further branches, so the structure can follow records
at additional depths. RelFlow generates the neural architecture from this
tree, with the retirement objective attached to the entry at its root:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.sm(
    driver_nationality=rf.Category,
    upcoming_circuit=rf.Category,
    constructor=rf.Category,
    past_results=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        occurred_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        age_days=rf.Number,
        circuit=rf.Category,
        constructor=rf.Category,
        grid_position=rf.Number,
        finishing_position=rf.Number,
        retired=rf.Boolean,
        pit_stops=rf.Branch(
            length=4,
            overflow="tail",
            lap=rf.Number,
            duration_seconds=rf.Number,
        ),
    ),
    retired_next_race=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

Order earlier results oldest to newest and each pit-stop collection by lap.
The illustrative caps retain the latest 32 results and latest four stops per
retained result. The schema describes the prepared nested input; it does not
discover database joins or enforce the historical availability contract.
Relationships enter as attributes and nested record collections assembled by
the application. The model consumes the resulting tree.

The `retired` fields describe earlier races and can be inputs. The separate
`retired_next_race` target is always masked and is omitted from prediction
requests. Calendar parts express periodic context; application-supplied
`age_days` expresses elapsed time to the cutoff. See
[Nested context and account outcomes](../learn/nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd)
for how targets and context can live at different tree levels.

## Test whether the related records help

Compare the nested model with the training-label retirement rate, a simple
driver-history baseline, and a flat model using recent results and constructor
history. Compare a version without pit stops to measure whether that extra
collection helps. All variants need the same scoring entries, cutoffs, label
availability, and training and evaluation periods.

Split by later races and decision times, keeping all entries for one race in
the same split. Report AUROC, average precision, calibration, and precision
or recall at the team's review budget. Report label coverage as well: removing
cancelled races and unavailable results changes which entries contribute to
the evaluation. Performance on familiar drivers and circuits does not establish
performance on new ones. See [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd).

Preserve both event time and availability time in the preparation pipeline.
A result amended after the cutoff cannot contribute its amended value to that
observation. Version mutable entry and constructor data, retain deterministic
join keys, and inspect row counts after every join. History caps and nested
fan-out require explicit resource budgets; a small root batch can still
contain many child records. [Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd),
[Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessing.qmd), and
[Performance](../guides/performance.qmd) cover these preparation and capacity
decisions.

## Adapt the entity and its related records

The same preparation pattern supports other multi-table questions. A retail
customer can own purchases with article attributes; a community member can own
posts whose comments and votes remain nested under each post. The important
choices are the scored entity, its cutoff, which relationships may contribute
context, and the meaning of its later label.

An **observational study-reporting** variant uses a study as the root, with
known study attributes, conditions, sponsors, and earlier reports as context.
For studies already started, define a 365-day numeric target as the sum of
`subjects_affected` in reports marked `serious` or `deaths` that arrive after
the cutoff through 365 days later. This adapts
[RelBench's study-adverse definition](https://github.com/snap-stanford/relbench/blob/v1.1.0/relbench/tasks/trial.py#L74-L122).
Compare a training-label median and a baseline using earlier report totals,
then assess MAE on later fully observed reporting windows.

That total can count a person in multiple reports. It measures reported
affected-subject totals, rather than unique affected people or individual
risk. Use report availability dates, version study attributes, and distinguish
missing reporting from a verified zero. Define which studies have complete
outcome windows before evaluating the task.

For a customer-level decision, continue with
[Customer outcomes](customer-outcomes.qmd). For a future sequence of numeric
values, see [Time series forecasting](time-series-forecasting.qmd); for a
ranked set of candidates, see [Recommendations](recommendations.qmd).
